claim: The anamniote lateral line system comprises mechanosensory neuromasts and electrosensory ampullary organs.
source: The anamniote lateral line system, comprising mechanosensory neuromasts and electrosensory ampullary organs, is a useful model for investigating the developmental and evolutionary diversification of different organs and cell types.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the composition of the lateral line system, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Neither zebrafish nor Xenopus is electroreceptive.
source: Zebrafish neuromast development is increasingly well understood, but neither zebrafish nor Xenopus is electroreceptive and our molecular understanding of ampullary organ development is rudimentary.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field about these model organisms.

claim: Transcription factor genes critical for hair cell development are expressed in developing ampullary organs of paddlefish.
source: Validation of a subset reveals expression in developing ampullary organs of transcription factor genes critical for hair cell development, and genes essential for glutamate release at hair cell ribbon synapses, suggesting close developmental, physiological and evolutionary links between non-teleost electroreceptors and hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Genes essential for glutamate release at hair cell ribbon synapses are expressed in developing ampullary organs of paddlefish.
source: Validation of a subset reveals expression in developing ampullary organs of transcription factor genes critical for hair cell development, and genes essential for glutamate release at hair cell ribbon synapses, suggesting close developmental, physiological and evolutionary links between non-teleost electroreceptors and hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: There are close developmental, physiological and evolutionary links between non-teleost electroreceptors and hair cells.
source: Validation of a subset reveals expression in developing ampullary organs of transcription factor genes critical for hair cell development, and genes essential for glutamate release at hair cell ribbon synapses, suggesting close developmental, physiological and evolutionary links between non-teleost electroreceptors and hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data showing shared molecular mechanisms between electroreceptors and hair cells.

claim: An ampullary organ-specific proneural transcription factor has been identified in paddlefish.
source: We identify an ampullary organ-specific proneural transcription factor, and candidates for the voltage-sensing L-type Cav channel and rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate (cartilaginous fish) ampullary organ electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing Neurod4 expression specifically in ampullary organs but not neuromasts.

claim: Candidates for the voltage-sensing L-type Cav channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology have been identified.
source: We identify an ampullary organ-specific proneural transcription factor, and candidates for the voltage-sensing L-type Cav channel and rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate (cartilaginous fish) ampullary organ electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data showing Cacna1d expression in ampullary organs, combined with inference from electrophysiology studies.

claim: Candidates for the rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology have been identified.
source: We identify an ampullary organ-specific proneural transcription factor, and candidates for the voltage-sensing L-type Cav channel and rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate (cartilaginous fish) ampullary organ electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data showing Kcna5 and Kcnab3 expression in ampullary organs, combined with inference from electrophysiology studies.

claim: In jawed vertebrates, mechanosensory neuromasts and electrosensory ampullary organs develop together with their afferent neurons from individual embryonic lateral line placodes.
source: In jawed vertebrates, this sensory system ancestrally includes mechanosensory neuromasts and electrosensory ampullary organs ('ampullae of Lorenzini'), both of which develop - together with their afferent neurons - from individual embryonic lateral line placodes (Northcutt et al., 1995; Modrell et al., 2011a; Gillis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Lampreys have neuromasts and electroreceptors, but the electroreceptors are collected in 'end buds' at the surface rather than recessed in ampullary organs.
source: (The jawless lampreys have neuromasts and electroreceptors, but the latter are collected in 'end buds' at the surface, rather than recessed in ampullary organs, and their embryonic origin is unknown; the lateral line system of hagfishes, which lack electroreceptors altogether, is secondarily reduced; Braun, 1996; Braun and Northcutt, 1997.)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The embryonic origin of lamprey electroreceptors is unknown.
source: (The jawless lampreys have neuromasts and electroreceptors, but the latter are collected in 'end buds' at the surface, rather than recessed in ampullary organs, and their embryonic origin is unknown; the lateral line system of hagfishes, which lack electroreceptors altogether, is secondarily reduced; Braun, 1996; Braun and Northcutt, 1997.)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Hagfishes lack electroreceptors altogether and their lateral line system is secondarily reduced.
source: (The jawless lampreys have neuromasts and electroreceptors, but the latter are collected in 'end buds' at the surface, rather than recessed in ampullary organs, and their embryonic origin is unknown; the lateral line system of hagfishes, which lack electroreceptors altogether, is secondarily reduced; Braun, 1996; Braun and Northcutt, 1997.)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The electrosensory division of the lateral line system was lost independently in the lineages leading to extant neopterygian fishes.
source: The electrosensory division of the lateral line system was lost independently in the lineages leading to extant neopterygian fishes (gars, bowfin and teleosts) and to anuran amphibians (neither of the major anamniote lab models, i.e., the teleost zebrafish and the frog Xenopus, has electroreceptors).
evidence: This claim is based on established evolutionary knowledge in the field.

claim: The electrosensory division of the lateral line system was lost independently in the lineage leading to anuran amphibians.
source: The electrosensory division of the lateral line system was lost independently in the lineages leading to extant neopterygian fishes (gars, bowfin and teleosts) and to anuran amphibians (neither of the major anamniote lab models, i.e., the teleost zebrafish and the frog Xenopus, has electroreceptors).
evidence: This claim is based on established evolutionary knowledge in the field.

claim: Electrosensory lateral line organs evolved independently at least twice within the teleosts, most likely from neuromast hair cells.
source: However, electrosensory lateral line organs evolved independently at least twice within the teleosts, most likely from neuromast hair cells (Bullock et al., 1983; Northcutt, 1986; Bodznick, 1989; Alves-Gomes, 2001; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Kawasaki, 2009; Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: The entire lateral line system was lost in amniotes with the transition to life on land.
source: The entire lateral line system was lost in amniotes, with the transition to life on land.
evidence: This claim is based on established evolutionary knowledge in the field.

claim: Ampullary organ development must be genetically separable from neuromast development.
source: The loss of the electrosensory division of the lateral line system in different vertebrate lineages shows that ampullary organ development must be genetically separable from neuromast development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the evolutionary pattern of independent losses of electroreceptors.

claim: Within the same lateral line placode-derived sensory ridge, neuromasts form first along the center of the ridge, while ampullary organs form later on the flanks.
source: Indeed, even within the same lateral line placode-derived sensory ridge, neuromasts form first, along the center of the ridge, while ampullary organs form later, on the flanks (Schlosser, 2002; Northcutt, 2005a; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Neuromasts contain mechanosensory hair cells plus supporting cells that secrete a gelatinous cupula.
source: Neuromasts and ampullary organs are morphologically distinct: neuromasts contain mechanosensory hair cells, plus supporting cells that secrete a gelatinous cupula; ampullary organs comprise a sensory epithelium of electroreceptor and supporting cells located at the base of a duct filled with conductive jelly, leading to a surface pore (Northcutt, 1986; Jørgensen, 2005; Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies describing the morphology of these structures.

claim: Ampullary organs comprise a sensory epithelium of electroreceptor and supporting cells located at the base of a duct filled with conductive jelly, leading to a surface pore.
source: Neuromasts and ampullary organs are morphologically distinct: neuromasts contain mechanosensory hair cells, plus supporting cells that secrete a gelatinous cupula; ampullary organs comprise a sensory epithelium of electroreceptor and supporting cells located at the base of a duct filled with conductive jelly, leading to a surface pore (Northcutt, 1986; Jørgensen, 2005; Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies describing the morphology of these structures.

claim: Ampullary electroreceptor cells generally have an apical primary cilium but either no or few apical microvilli, which are not organized into the 'hair bundle' that characterizes hair cells.
source: Ampullary electroreceptor cells generally have an apical primary cilium but either no or few apical microvilli, which are not organized into the 'hair bundle' (stair-case array) that characterizes hair cells (Northcutt, 1986; Jørgensen, 2005; Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies describing the cellular morphology.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying neuromast formation from the migrating posterior lateral line primordium in zebrafish have been intensively studied.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying neuromast formation from the migrating posterior lateral line primordium in zebrafish have been intensively studied (Chitnis et al., 2012; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Thomas et al., 2015), but our molecular understanding of ampullary organ development is very limited.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Our molecular understanding of ampullary organ development is very limited.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying neuromast formation from the migrating posterior lateral line primordium in zebrafish have been intensively studied (Chitnis et al., 2012; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Thomas et al., 2015), but our molecular understanding of ampullary organ development is very limited.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the contrast with zebrafish neuromast studies.

claim: All vertebrate electroreceptors have electron-dense pre-synaptic bodies surrounded by a large pool of synaptic vesicles, like hair cells, retinal and pineal photoreceptors, and retinal bipolar neurons.
source: Like hair cells (and also retinal and pineal photoreceptors, and retinal bipolar neurons), all vertebrate electroreceptors have electron-dense pre-synaptic bodies surrounded by a large pool of synaptic vesicles (Northcutt, 1986; Jørgensen, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Ribbon synapses respond to graded signals and are capable of sustained neurotransmitter release.
source: Such 'ribbon synapses' respond to graded signals and are capable of sustained neurotransmitter release (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Pangršič et al., 2012; Safieddine et al., 2012; Nicolson, 2015; Wichmann and Moser, 2015; Moser and Starr, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: In dissected skate ampullary organs, activation of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels results in the release of a 'glutamate-like' neurotransmitter.
source: While the specific proteins involved in ribbon synapse function are increasingly understood in retinal photoreceptors and hair cells (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Pangršič et al., 2012; Safieddine et al., 2012; Nicolson, 2015; Wichmann and Moser, 2015; Moser and Starr, 2016), all that is known about neurotransmission at non-teleost electroreceptor ribbon synapses is from work in dissected skate (cartilaginous fish) ampullary organs, which showed that activation of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels results in the release of a 'glutamate-like' neurotransmitter (Bennett and Obara, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous electrophysiology research.

claim: Current- and voltage-clamp approaches to study epithelial currents in dissected single ampullary organ preparations from skates revealed that L-type voltage-gated calcium channels are required both for voltage-sensing in the apical electroreceptor membrane and for neurotransmitter release basally.
source: Similarly, our only detailed understanding of non-teleost ampullary organ physiology until very recently had come from current- and voltage-clamp approaches to study epithelial currents in dissected single ampullary organ preparations from skates (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005). These revealed that L-type voltage-gated calcium channels are required both for voltage-sensing in the apical (lumenal, i.e., exterior-facing) electroreceptor membrane, and for neurotransmitter release basally.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology research.

claim: The basal membrane of skate electroreceptors is repolarized by voltage-gated potassium channels and calcium-dependent chloride channels.
source: The basal membrane is repolarized by voltage-gated potassium channels and calcium-dependent chloride channels, while the apical membrane is repolarized by the calcium-gated potassium channel BK (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; King et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology research.

claim: The apical membrane of skate electroreceptors is repolarized by the calcium-gated potassium channel BK.
source: The basal membrane is repolarized by voltage-gated potassium channels and calcium-dependent chloride channels, while the apical membrane is repolarized by the calcium-gated potassium channel BK (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; King et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology research.

claim: BK was cloned directly from skate ampullary organs a little over 40 years after its properties were initially discovered using the same preparation.
source: BK was recently cloned directly from skate ampullary organs (King et al., 2016), a little over 40 years after its properties were initially discovered using the same preparation (Clusin et al., 1975; Clusin and Bennett, 1977a; Clusin and Bennett, 1977b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp experiments on dissociated electroreceptors from adult skates, together with transcriptome profiling, revealed that the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 mediates the low-threshold voltage-activated inward current and works together with BK to mediate electroreceptor membrane oscillations.
source: While the current manuscript was under review, whole-cell patch-clamp experiments on dissociated electroreceptors from adult skates, together with transcriptome profiling, revealed that the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 mediates the low-threshold voltage-activated inward current, and works together with BK to mediate electroreceptor membrane oscillations (Bellono et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent research study.

claim: The specific ion channels and subunits involved in electroreceptor function have not been identified in any vertebrate, except for recent work on Cav1.3 in skate.
source: Other than this recent exciting advance (Bellono et al., 2017), the specific ion channels and subunits involved in electroreceptor function have not been identified in any vertebrate.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Our understanding of the specific molecular basis of both vertebrate electroreceptor development and physiology is still rudimentary.
source: In short, our understanding of the specific molecular basis of both vertebrate electroreceptor development and physiology is still rudimentary.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Candidate gene approaches have identified some transcription factors and a few other genes expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in larval axolotl, paddlefish, shark and skate.
source: The few candidate gene approaches reported thus far have identified some transcription factors, and a few other genes, expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in larval axolotl (Metscher et al., 1997; Modrell and Baker, 2012), paddlefish (Modrell et al., 2011a, 2011b; Butts et al., 2014), shark and skate (Freitas et al., 2006; Gillis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: A candidate gene approach will not identify genes important specifically for ampullary organ development or function.
source: However, a candidate gene approach will not identify genes important specifically for ampullary organ development or function.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of candidate gene approaches.

claim: Transcriptomes were generated at stage 46 from pooled paddlefish opercula versus fins.
source: We generated transcriptomes at stage 46 (the onset of independent feeding; Bemis and Grande, 1992) from pooled paddlefish opercula (gill-flaps), which are covered in ampullary organs plus some neuromasts, versus fins, which have a generally similar tissue composition but no lateral line organs at all (Modrell et al., 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Paddlefish opercula are covered in ampullary organs plus some neuromasts.
source: We generated transcriptomes at stage 46 (the onset of independent feeding; Bemis and Grande, 1992) from pooled paddlefish opercula (gill-flaps), which are covered in ampullary organs plus some neuromasts, versus fins, which have a generally similar tissue composition but no lateral line organs at all (Modrell et al., 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Paddlefish fins have a generally similar tissue composition to opercula but no lateral line organs at all.
source: We generated transcriptomes at stage 46 (the onset of independent feeding; Bemis and Grande, 1992) from pooled paddlefish opercula (gill-flaps), which are covered in ampullary organs plus some neuromasts, versus fins, which have a generally similar tissue composition but no lateral line organs at all (Modrell et al., 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Differential expression analysis yielded 490 genes, excluding duplicates, enriched at least 1.85-fold in operculum versus fin tissue.
source: Differential expression analysis yielded 490 genes, excluding duplicates, enriched at least 1.85-fold (log2fold 0.89) in operculum versus fin tissue, hereafter designated 'lateral line-enriched' (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the results of the differential expression analysis performed in the study.

claim: Of the 490 lateral line-enriched genes, 112 were uncharacterized loci or could only be assigned to a protein family.
source: Of these genes, 112 were uncharacterized loci or could only be assigned to a protein family, while a further 44 were described as being 'like' a specific gene, leaving 334 assigned genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the annotation results of the lateral line-enriched genes.

claim: Binding activities represent approximately 39% of the function hits in the lateral line-enriched dataset.
source: Binding activities GO:0005488 (blue) represent ~39% of the function hits (16% nucleic acid binding GO:0003637; 17% protein binding GO:0005515; 6% other binding, including calcium and lipid binding).
evidence: This is supported by the Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Catalytic activities account for approximately 35% of the function hits in the lateral line-enriched dataset.
source: Catalytic activities GO:0003824 (green) account for ~35% of the function hits (4% enzyme regulator activity GO:0030234; 9% transferase; and 11% each hydrolase and other catalytic activities).
evidence: This is supported by the Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Transmembrane-associated activities represent approximately 19% of function hits in the lateral line-enriched dataset.
source: Transmembrane-associated activities (orange) represent ~19% of function hits (13% transporter GO:0005215; 6% receptor GO:0004872).
evidence: This is supported by the Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lateral line-enriched dataset includes Six1 and Six2, whose expression was previously reported in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in larval paddlefish.
source: The lateral line-enriched dataset (Supplementary file 1) includes several transcription factor genes whose expression we had previously reported in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in larval paddlefish, suggesting that the differential expression analysis had been successful. These were: the homeodomain transcription factor genes Six1 and Six2 (Modrell et al., 2011a); the HMG-domain SoxB1 class transcription factor gene Sox3 (Modrell et al., 2011b); and the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor gene Atoh1, whose lateral line organ expression at stages 40–45 was noted, in passing, in a study on cerebellum development (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The lateral line-enriched dataset includes Sox3, whose expression was previously reported in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in larval paddlefish.
source: The lateral line-enriched dataset (Supplementary file 1) includes several transcription factor genes whose expression we had previously reported in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in larval paddlefish, suggesting that the differential expression analysis had been successful. These were: the homeodomain transcription factor genes Six1 and Six2 (Modrell et al., 2011a); the HMG-domain SoxB1 class transcription factor gene Sox3 (Modrell et al., 2011b); and the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor gene Atoh1, whose lateral line organ expression at stages 40–45 was noted, in passing, in a study on cerebellum development (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The lateral line-enriched dataset includes Atoh1, whose lateral line organ expression at stages 40-45 was noted in a study on cerebellum development.
source: The lateral line-enriched dataset (Supplementary file 1) includes several transcription factor genes whose expression we had previously reported in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in larval paddlefish, suggesting that the differential expression analysis had been successful. These were: the homeodomain transcription factor genes Six1 and Six2 (Modrell et al., 2011a); the HMG-domain SoxB1 class transcription factor gene Sox3 (Modrell et al., 2011b); and the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor gene Atoh1, whose lateral line organ expression at stages 40–45 was noted, in passing, in a study on cerebellum development (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Atoh1 is essential for hair cell formation.
source: Atoh1 is essential for hair cell formation (Bermingham et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Paddlefish Atoh1 is 18.6-fold lateral line-enriched.
source: Paddlefish Atoh1 is 18.6-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1), and expressed by stage 33 within the otic and preopercular neuromast canal lines (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Paddlefish Atoh1 is expressed by stage 33 within the otic and preopercular neuromast canal lines.
source: Paddlefish Atoh1 is 18.6-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1), and expressed by stage 33 within the otic and preopercular neuromast canal lines (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Paddlefish Atoh1 is expressed within most canal lines and the migrating posterior lateral line primordium by stage 37.
source: It is expressed within most canal lines and the migrating posterior lateral line primordium by stage 37 (Figure 2B), and in the developing ampullary organ fields by stage 39 (Figure 2C), where it persists at stage 46 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Paddlefish Atoh1 is expressed in the developing ampullary organ fields by stage 39.
source: It is expressed within most canal lines and the migrating posterior lateral line primordium by stage 37 (Figure 2B), and in the developing ampullary organ fields by stage 39 (Figure 2C), where it persists at stage 46 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Paddlefish Atoh1 expression persists in ampullary organ fields at stage 46.
source: It is expressed within most canal lines and the migrating posterior lateral line primordium by stage 37 (Figure 2B), and in the developing ampullary organ fields by stage 39 (Figure 2C), where it persists at stage 46 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In mouse cochlear explants, Six1 and its co-factor Eya1, acting cooperatively with Sox2, are sufficient to induce Atoh1.
source: In mouse cochlear explants, Six1 and its co-factor Eya1, acting cooperatively with SoxB1 subfamily member Sox2, are sufficient to induce Atoh1 (Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Eya1 is expressed in paddlefish ampullary organs.
source: Like Six1, Eya1 is also expressed in paddlefish ampullary organs (Modrell et al., 2011a), while Sox2 is 3.3-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sox2 is 3.3-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Like Six1, Eya1 is also expressed in paddlefish ampullary organs (Modrell et al., 2011a), while Sox2 is 3.3-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Immunostaining with a cross-reactive anti-Sox2 antibody revealed Sox2 expression in developing ampullary organs as well as neuromasts in paddlefish.
source: Immunostaining with a cross-reactive anti-Sox2 antibody revealed Sox2 expression in developing ampullary organs as well as neuromasts (Figure 2E–H), consistent with Sox2 mRNA expression by in situ hybridization (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: Sox2 represses Atoh1 in supporting cells in the mouse cochlea.
source: Sox2 represses Atoh1 in supporting cells in the mouse cochlea while, conversely, Atoh1 represses Sox2 in developing hair cells (Dabdoub et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Atoh1 represses Sox2 in developing hair cells in the mouse cochlea.
source: Sox2 represses Atoh1 in supporting cells in the mouse cochlea while, conversely, Atoh1 represses Sox2 in developing hair cells (Dabdoub et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: By stage 46, paddlefish Atoh1 expression is hard to detect in canal neuromasts but is still strong in ampullary organs.
source: By stage 46, paddlefish Atoh1 expression is hard to detect in canal neuromasts - perhaps partly due to strong expression in scattered overlying epidermal cells, presumably Merkel cells (Maricich et al., 2009; Whitear, 1989) - but is still strong in ampullary organs (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Sox2 immunoreactivity remains strong in both neuromasts and ampullary organs at stage 46 in paddlefish.
source: Sox2 immunoreactivity remains strong in both neuromasts and ampullary organs at stage 46 (Figure 2J), where it is most likely restricted to supporting cells, given its punctate staining pattern.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Sox2 is most likely restricted to supporting cells in paddlefish lateral line organs at stage 46, given its punctate staining pattern.
source: Sox2 immunoreactivity remains strong in both neuromasts and ampullary organs at stage 46 (Figure 2J), where it is most likely restricted to supporting cells, given its punctate staining pattern.
evidence: This is an inference based on the staining pattern observed in the data.

claim: Of the 66 genes in the lateral line-enriched dataset that encode known transcription factors, Pou4f3 was the top candidate.
source: Of the 66 genes in the lateral line-enriched dataset that encode known transcription factors (three other transcription factor genes in the dataset were assigned only to families) (Supplementary file 1), our top candidate was Pou4f3 (Brn3c, DFNA15), which is 27.5-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Pou4f3 is 27.5-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Of the 66 genes in the lateral line-enriched dataset that encode known transcription factors (three other transcription factor genes in the dataset were assigned only to families) (Supplementary file 1), our top candidate was Pou4f3 (Brn3c, DFNA15), which is 27.5-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Pou4f3 is a confirmed Atoh1 target in hair cells.
source: Pou4f3 is a confirmed Atoh1 target in hair cells (Masuda et al., 2011; Ikeda et al., 2015) and required for hearing (Costaridis et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pou4f3 is required for hearing.
source: Pou4f3 is a confirmed Atoh1 target in hair cells (Masuda et al., 2011; Ikeda et al., 2015) and required for hearing (Costaridis et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In mouse cochlear explants, Six1 and Eya1, acting independently of Atoh1, are sufficient to induce Pou4f3, which promotes hair cell differentiation.
source: In mouse cochlear explants, Six1 and Eya1 - acting independently of Atoh1 - are sufficient to induce Pou4f3, which promotes hair cell differentiation (Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Paddlefish Pou4f3 is expressed in ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
source: Like Atoh1, paddlefish Pou4f3 is expressed in ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts (Figure 2K,L).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2K,L.

claim: All three SoxB1 subfamily genes are putative Atoh1 targets in the postnatal mouse cerebellum and present in the lateral line-enriched dataset.
source: All three SoxB1 subfamily genes are putative Atoh1 targets in the postnatal mouse cerebellum (Klisch et al., 2011) and present in the lateral line-enriched dataset.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and the dataset.

claim: Sox3 is 5.2-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Sox3 is 5.2-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1); as noted above, we previously reported its expression in paddlefish ampullary organs and neuromasts (Modrell et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Sox1 is 8.6-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Sox1 is 8.6-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1) and expressed in ampullary organs from their eruption (Figure 2M–P).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Paddlefish Sox1 is expressed in ampullary organs from their eruption.
source: Sox1 is 8.6-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1) and expressed in ampullary organs from their eruption (Figure 2M–P).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2M-P.

claim: Paddlefish Sox1 is transiently expressed in the migrating posterior lateral line primordium.
source: It is transiently expressed in the migrating posterior lateral line primordium (Figure 2M,N) and, at later stages, expression is also seen in neuromast canal lines (Figure 2O,P).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2M,N.

claim: At later stages, paddlefish Sox1 expression is also seen in neuromast canal lines.
source: It is transiently expressed in the migrating posterior lateral line primordium (Figure 2M,N) and, at later stages, expression is also seen in neuromast canal lines (Figure 2O,P).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2O,P.

claim: The transcriptional network regulating the development of both lateral line organ types is likely to be highly conserved, including the likely requirement of Atoh1 for electroreceptor as well as hair cell formation.
source: Taken together, these data support a high degree of conservation in the transcriptional network regulating the development of both lateral line organ types, including the likely requirement of Atoh1 for electroreceptor as well as hair cell formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data showing shared transcription factors.

claim: Neurod4 is 18.9-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Another highly lateral line-enriched transcription factor gene is Neurod4 (Ath3, NeuroM) (18.9-fold enriched; Supplementary file 1), a putative cerebellar Atoh1 target (Klisch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Lhx3 is a putative cerebellar Atoh1 target gene.
source: Lhx3 is expressed in all inner ear hair cells, although its expression is differentially regulated by Pou4f3 in cochlear versus vestibular hair cells (Hertzano et al., 2007); it is also a putative cerebellar Atoh1 target gene (Klisch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Lhx3 is 16.3-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.

claim: Paddlefish Lhx3 is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.

source: Hence, it is possible that Lhx3 could interact with Neurod4 in paddlefish ampullary organs to specify electroreceptors, and with another partner in neuromasts to specify hair cells.
