evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Myt1 is 6.1-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Finally, we examined the zinc finger transcription factor gene Myt1, another putative cerebellar Atoh1 target gene (Klisch et al., 2011) that is 6.1-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Myt1 expression is upregulated in Xenopus embryos by Neurod4.
source: We selected Myt1 because its expression is upregulated in Xenopus embryos by Neurod4 (Perron et al., 1999; Hardwick and Philpott, 2015), and it synergizes with Neurod4 to induce neuronal differentiation in this system (Perron et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Myt1 synergizes with Neurod4 to induce neuronal differentiation in Xenopus.
source: We selected Myt1 because its expression is upregulated in Xenopus embryos by Neurod4 (Perron et al., 1999; Hardwick and Philpott, 2015), and it synergizes with Neurod4 to induce neuronal differentiation in this system (Perron et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Myt1 transcripts are reportedly enriched in both cochlear and vestibular hair cells in postnatal mice.
source: Furthermore, Myt1 transcripts are reportedly enriched in both cochlear and vestibular hair cells in postnatal mice (Elkon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Paddlefish Myt1 is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: We found expression of paddlefish Myt1 in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The transcription factor networks underlying hair cell development, which center around Atoh1, are likely to be active in paddlefish ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
source: Overall, our results suggest that the transcription factor networks underlying hair cell development, which center around Atoh1, are likely to be active in paddlefish ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data showing shared transcription factors.

claim: There is significant conservation between the molecular mechanisms underlying hair cell and electroreceptor development.
source: This suggests significant conservation between the molecular mechanisms underlying hair cell and electroreceptor development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the shared expression of developmental genes.

claim: The unbiased RNA-seq approach has identified the first transcription factor gene expressed in ampullary organs but not neuromasts, Neurod4.
source: Furthermore, our unbiased RNA-seq approach has also identified the first transcription factor gene expressed in ampullary organs but not neuromasts, Neurod4.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from the RNA-seq and validation studies.

claim: Neurod4 may be involved in specifying ampullary organ and/or electroreceptor fate in paddlefish.
source: Given the importance of members of the proneural bHLH Neurod family for specifying cell fate, we suggest that Neurod4 may be involved in specifying ampullary organ and/or electroreceptor fate in paddlefish.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential expression pattern and known functions of Neurod family members.

claim: Some of the most highly lateral line-enriched genes in the paddlefish dataset are required for synaptic transmission in hair cells.
source: Some of the most highly lateral line-enriched genes in our paddlefish dataset are required for synaptic transmission in hair cells, which occurs at specialized 'ribbon synapses' characterized by electron-dense, pre-synaptic structures called 'synaptic ribbons' (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Pangršič et al., 2012; Safieddine et al., 2012; Nicolson, 2015; Wichmann and Moser, 2015; Moser and Starr, 2016).
evidence: This is based on the dataset and citations to previous research on hair cell synaptic transmission.

claim: Synaptic ribbons tether glutamate-filled synaptic vesicles and stabilize L-type voltage-gated calcium channels at the plasma membrane.
source: These tether glutamate-filled synaptic vesicles and stabilize L-type voltage-gated calcium channels at the plasma membrane (Cav1.3 in hair cells; Cav1.4, in retinal photoreceptors; Joiner and Lee, 2015), enabling rapid and sustained glutamate release in response to activation of these calcium channels by membrane depolarization (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Pangršič et al., 2012; Safieddine et al., 2012; Nicolson, 2015; Wichmann and Moser, 2015; Moser and Starr, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Electroreceptors have synaptic ribbons of varying morphology.
source: Electroreceptors also have synaptic ribbons of varying morphology (Northcutt, 1986; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005): in paddlefish, they were described as synaptic 'sheets' (Jorgensen et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In paddlefish, electroreceptor synaptic ribbons were described as synaptic 'sheets'.
source: Electroreceptors also have synaptic ribbons of varying morphology (Northcutt, 1986; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005): in paddlefish, they were described as synaptic 'sheets' (Jorgensen et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In hair cells, glutamate is loaded into synaptic vesicles by the vesicular glutamate transporter Vglut3, which is encoded by Slc17a8 and essential for hair cell synaptic transmission in mouse and zebrafish.
source: In hair cells, glutamate is loaded into synaptic vesicles by the vesicular glutamate transporter Vglut3, which is encoded by Slc17a8 (DFNA25) and essential for hair cell synaptic transmission in mouse (Ruel et al., 2008; Seal et al., 2008) and zebrafish (Obholzer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Vglut1 or Vglut2 are used at glutamatergic synapses in the central nervous system, and at photoreceptor and bipolar cell ribbon synapses.
source: This is unusual: Vglut1 or Vglut2 are used at glutamatergic synapses in the central nervous system, and at photoreceptor and bipolar cell ribbon synapses (see e.g. Zanazzi and Matthews, 2009; Pangršič et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Slc17a8 is 30.9-fold enriched in the paddlefish lateral line-enriched dataset.
source: Slc17a8 is one of the most highly enriched genes in our paddlefish dataset (30.9-fold enriched; Supplementary file 1), and proved to be expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Paddlefish Slc17a8 is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Slc17a8 is one of the most highly enriched genes in our paddlefish dataset (30.9-fold enriched; Supplementary file 1), and proved to be expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Synaptic vesicles in electroreceptors are likely to be loaded by the same vesicular glutamate transporter as hair cells.
source: Hence, synaptic vesicles in electroreceptors are likely to be loaded by the same vesicular glutamate transporter as hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of Slc17a8 in both cell types.

claim: The afferent neurotransmitter released by non-teleost electroreceptors is indeed glutamate, as in hair cells.
source: Furthermore, this also provides independent evidence that the afferent neurotransmitter released by non-teleost electroreceptors is indeed glutamate, as in hair cells (and photoreceptors), as suggested by electrophysiology experiments on dissected skate ampullary organs (Bennett and Obara, 1986).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of Slc17a8 and supported by previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: Hair cells are thought to be unique in depending on the multi-C2 domain transmembrane protein otoferlin for synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
source: Hair cells are thought to be unique in depending on the multi-C2 domain transmembrane protein otoferlin for synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Yasunaga et al., 1999; Roux et al., 2006; Pangršič et al., 2010; Chatterjee et al., 2015; Strenzke et al., 2016; Vogl et al., 2016), rather than neuronal SNAREs (Nouvian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hair cells use otoferlin rather than neuronal SNAREs for synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
source: Hair cells are thought to be unique in depending on the multi-C2 domain transmembrane protein otoferlin for synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Yasunaga et al., 1999; Roux et al., 2006; Pangršič et al., 2010; Chatterjee et al., 2015; Strenzke et al., 2016; Vogl et al., 2016), rather than neuronal SNAREs (Nouvian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hair cells contrast with all other ribbon synapses in their use of otoferlin rather than neuronal SNAREs.
source: This contrasts not only with conventional synapses but also with all other ribbon synapses (see e.g. Zanazzi and Matthews, 2009; Mercer and Thoreson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Otoferlin is a type II ferlin encoded by Otof.
source: Otoferlin is a type II ferlin (Lek et al., 2012) encoded by Otof (DFNAB6, DFNAB9), which is 20.9-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Otof is 20.9-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Otoferlin is a type II ferlin (Lek et al., 2012) encoded by Otof (DFNAB6, DFNAB9), which is 20.9-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Paddlefish Otof is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Otof is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts in paddlefish (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Synaptic vesicle exocytosis at the electroreceptor ribbon synapse is likely otoferlin-dependent, just as at the hair cell ribbon synapse.
source: This suggests that synaptic vesicle exocytosis at the electroreceptor ribbon synapse, just as at the hair cell ribbon synapse, is otoferlin-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of Otof in both cell types.

claim: The L-type voltage-gated calcium channel whose opening triggers synaptic vesicle exocytosis in hair cells is Cav1.3.
source: The L-type voltage-gated calcium channel whose opening triggers synaptic vesicle exocytosis in hair cells is Cav1.3 (Kollmar et al., 1997; Platzer et al., 2000; Brandt et al., 2003; Michna et al., 2003; Dou et al., 2004; Brandt et al., 2005; Baig et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Retinal photoreceptors express Cav1.3 but rely on Cav1.4 for calcium influx.
source: This contrasts with retinal photoreceptors, which do express Cav1.3, but rely on Cav1.4 for calcium influx (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Joiner and Lee, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The pore-forming alpha subunit of Cav1.3 is encoded by Cacna1d, which is required for hearing.
source: The pore-forming (alpha) subunit of Cav1.3 is encoded by Cacna1d, which is required for hearing (Platzer et al., 2000; Dou et al., 2004; Baig et al., 2011), and also for hair cell function in zebrafish (Nicolson et al., 1998; Sidi et al., 2004), where it is expressed in both neuromasts and the inner ear (Sidi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cacna1d is required for hair cell function in zebrafish and is expressed in both neuromasts and the inner ear.
source: The pore-forming (alpha) subunit of Cav1.3 is encoded by Cacna1d, which is required for hearing (Platzer et al., 2000; Dou et al., 2004; Baig et al., 2011), and also for hair cell function in zebrafish (Nicolson et al., 1998; Sidi et al., 2004), where it is expressed in both neuromasts and the inner ear (Sidi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Zebrafish cacna1da is expressed in hair cells plus retinal photoreceptors, while cacna1db is expressed in retinal and pineal photoreceptors, but not hair cells.
source: (The two zebrafish cacna1d genes show differential expression: cacna1da is expressed in hair cells plus retinal photoreceptors, while cacna1db is expressed in retinal and pineal photoreceptors, but not hair cells; Sidi et al., 2004.)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Paddlefish Cacna1d is 19.3-fold lateral line-enriched.
source: Paddlefish Cacna1d is 19.3-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1) and expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Paddlefish Cacna1d is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Paddlefish Cacna1d is 19.3-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1) and expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cav1.3 channels in the basal membrane are likely to mediate glutamate release from both paddlefish electroreceptors and hair cells.
source: Hence, Cav1.3 channels in the basal membrane are likely to mediate glutamate release from both paddlefish electroreceptors and hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of Cacna1d in both cell types.

claim: The L-type voltage-gated calcium channels involved in neurotransmitter release from skate ampullary organs are likely to be Cav1.3 channels.
source: Given the homology of non-teleost ampullary organs (Bullock et al., 1983; Northcutt, 1986, Northcutt, 1992; Braun, 1996; New, 1997; Baker et al., 2013), this also suggests that the L-type voltage-gated calcium channels involved in neurotransmitter release from skate ampullary organs are likely to be Cav1.3 channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the homology of ampullary organs and the paddlefish data.

claim: The abundance and function of Cav1.3 channels in inner ear hair cells is regulated by the auxiliary beta subunit Cavβ2, which is required for hearing.
source: The abundance and function of Cav1.3 channels in inner ear hair cells is regulated by the auxiliary beta subunit Cavβ2, which is required for hearing (Neef et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cavβ2 is encoded by Cacnb2, which is the only other voltage-gated Ca2+ channel subunit gene in the lateral line-enriched dataset.
source: Cavβ2 is encoded by Cacnb2, which is the only other voltage-gated Ca2+ channel subunit gene in the lateral line-enriched dataset (2.7-fold enriched; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the dataset.

claim: Cacnb2 is 2.7-fold enriched in the paddlefish lateral line-enriched dataset.
source: Cavβ2 is encoded by Cacnb2, which is the only other voltage-gated Ca2+ channel subunit gene in the lateral line-enriched dataset (2.7-fold enriched; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Paddlefish Cacnb2 is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, with seemingly stronger expression in ampullary organs.
source: Although neuromast expression of cacnb2a and cacnb2b was not reported in zebrafish (Zhou et al., 2008), paddlefish Cacnb2 is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, with seemingly stronger expression in ampullary organs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cavβ2 may be the auxiliary beta-subunit for Cav1.3 channels in electroreceptors, as well as hair cells.
source: This suggests that Cavβ2 may be the auxiliary beta-subunit for Cav1.3 channels in electroreceptors, as well as hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and known function in hair cells.

claim: The voltage sensors in skate electroreceptors are L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane.
source: Furthermore, given that the voltage sensors in skate electroreceptors are L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005), recently demonstrated to be Cav1.3 channels (Bellono et al., 2017), and the fact that an apical calcium conductance is required for the firing of sturgeon ampullary organ afferents (Teeter et al., 1980), it seems likely that apically-located Cav1.3 channels, with Cavβ2 auxiliary beta subunits, act as the voltage-sensing channels, as well as mediating neurotransmitter release basally.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology research.

claim: The voltage sensors in skate electroreceptors were recently demonstrated to be Cav1.3 channels.
source: Furthermore, given that the voltage sensors in skate electroreceptors are L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005), recently demonstrated to be Cav1.3 channels (Bellono et al., 2017), and the fact that an apical calcium conductance is required for the firing of sturgeon ampullary organ afferents (Teeter et al., 1980), it seems likely that apically-located Cav1.3 channels, with Cavβ2 auxiliary beta subunits, act as the voltage-sensing channels, as well as mediating neurotransmitter release basally.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: An apical calcium conductance is required for the firing of sturgeon ampullary organ afferents.
source: Furthermore, given that the voltage sensors in skate electroreceptors are L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005), recently demonstrated to be Cav1.3 channels (Bellono et al., 2017), and the fact that an apical calcium conductance is required for the firing of sturgeon ampullary organ afferents (Teeter et al., 1980), it seems likely that apically-located Cav1.3 channels, with Cavβ2 auxiliary beta subunits, act as the voltage-sensing channels, as well as mediating neurotransmitter release basally.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It seems likely that apically-located Cav1.3 channels, with Cavβ2 auxiliary beta subunits, act as the voltage-sensing channels in paddlefish electroreceptors, as well as mediating neurotransmitter release basally.
source: Furthermore, given that the voltage sensors in skate electroreceptors are L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005), recently demonstrated to be Cav1.3 channels (Bellono et al., 2017), and the fact that an apical calcium conductance is required for the firing of sturgeon ampullary organ afferents (Teeter et al., 1980), it seems likely that apically-located Cav1.3 channels, with Cavβ2 auxiliary beta subunits, act as the voltage-sensing channels, as well as mediating neurotransmitter release basally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the paddlefish expression data and previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: Paddlefish Rims2 and Ctbp2 are expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Finally, we report the expression in both ampullary organs and neuromasts of Rims2 (Rim2) and Ctbp2 (Ribeye), which encode proteins associated with synaptic ribbons in photoreceptors as well as hair cells (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Pangršič et al., 2012; Safieddine et al., 2012; Nicolson, 2015; Wichmann and Moser, 2015) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Rims2 and Ctbp2 encode proteins associated with synaptic ribbons in photoreceptors as well as hair cells.
source: Finally, we report the expression in both ampullary organs and neuromasts of Rims2 (Rim2) and Ctbp2 (Ribeye), which encode proteins associated with synaptic ribbons in photoreceptors as well as hair cells (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Pangršič et al., 2012; Safieddine et al., 2012; Nicolson, 2015; Wichmann and Moser, 2015) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Rims2 encodes Rab3-interacting molecules 2α and β, which are required in cochlear inner hair cells for Cav1.3 channel recruitment to the active zone membrane beneath the synaptic ribbon.
source: Rims2 encodes Rab3-interacting molecules 2α and β, which are required in cochlear inner hair cells for Cav1.3 channel recruitment to the active zone membrane beneath the synaptic ribbon (Jung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Rims2 is 15.7-fold lateral line-enriched in paddlefish.
source: Rims2 is 15.7-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1) and expressed in all lateral line organs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Paddlefish Rims2 is expressed in all lateral line organs.
source: Rims2 is 15.7-fold lateral line-enriched (Supplementary file 1) and expressed in all lateral line organs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Rims2 may be involved in Cav1.3 channel recruitment in electroreceptors.
source: Hence, Rims2 may also be involved in Cav1.3 channel recruitment in electroreceptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and known function in hair cells.

claim: Ribeye is the only known synaptic ribbon-specific protein and is the main structural component of synaptic ribbons in both photoreceptors and hair cells.
source: Ribeye, the only known synaptic ribbon-specific protein, is the main structural component of synaptic ribbons in both photoreceptors and hair cells, encoded by usage of an alternative start site for the transcription factor gene Ctbp2 that generates an N-terminal A-domain unique to Ribeye (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Nicolson, 2015; Wichmann and Moser, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ribeye is important in zebrafish neuromast hair cells for Cav1.3 channel recruitment to synaptic ribbons and stabilizing synaptic contacts with afferent neurons.
source: Ribeye is important in zebrafish neuromast hair cells for Cav1.3 channel recruitment to synaptic ribbons and stabilizing synaptic contacts with afferent neurons (Sheets et al., 2011; Lv et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Deletion in mice of the exon encoding the Ribeye A-domain showed that Ribeye is essential in the retina both for ribbon formation per se, and for rapid and sustained neurotransmitter release.
source: Recently, deletion in mice of the exon encoding the A-domain showed that Ribeye is essential in the retina (the ear was not examined) both for ribbon formation per se, and for rapid and sustained neurotransmitter release (Maxeiner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Ctbp2 is not in the lateral line-enriched dataset, but was present in the combined transcriptome.
source: Ctbp2 is not in the lateral line-enriched dataset, but was present in the combined transcriptome, so was easily cloned.
evidence: This describes the presence of Ctbp2 in the transcriptome data.

claim: A riboprobe that exclusively recognizes the Ribeye-specific A-domain sequence of paddlefish Ctbp2 reveals expression in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: As expected, a riboprobe that exclusively recognizes the Ribeye-specific A-domain sequence of paddlefish Ctbp2 reveals expression in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 4F), suggesting that Ribeye is likely to be a key component of synaptic ribbons in electroreceptors (and hair cells), where it may also be important for Cav1.3 channel recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Ribeye is likely to be a key component of synaptic ribbons in electroreceptors and hair cells, where it may also be important for Cav1.3 channel recruitment.
source: As expected, a riboprobe that exclusively recognizes the Ribeye-specific A-domain sequence of paddlefish Ctbp2 reveals expression in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 4F), suggesting that Ribeye is likely to be a key component of synaptic ribbons in electroreceptors (and hair cells), where it may also be important for Cav1.3 channel recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and known function in hair cells.

claim: The mechanisms of neurotransmission at the ribbon synapse in paddlefish electroreceptors are essentially identical to those at the hair cell ribbon synapse, involving otoferlin-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles loaded with glutamate by Vglut3, in response to the activation of basal Cav1.3 channels.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the mechanisms of neurotransmission at the ribbon synapse in paddlefish electroreceptors are essentially identical to those at the hair cell ribbon synapse, involving otoferlin-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles, loaded with glutamate by Vglut3, in response to the activation of basal Cav1.3 channels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data showing shared synaptic transmission genes.

claim: These neurotransmission mechanisms are predicted to be conserved across all other non-teleost ampullary organs, since non-teleost ampullary organs are homologous.
source: Since non-teleost ampullary organs are homologous (Bullock et al., 1983; Northcutt, 1986, Northcutt, 1992; Braun, 1996; New, 1997; Baker et al., 2013), we predict that these mechanisms will be conserved across all other non-teleost ampullary organs.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the homology of ampullary organs and the paddlefish data.

claim: The paddlefish lateral line-enriched dataset contains two parvalbumin genes: one annotated as related to zebrafish 'pvalb8' is enriched 22.8-fold, and the other annotated as related to zebrafish 'pvalb3' is enriched 2.1-fold.
source: The paddlefish lateral line-enriched dataset contains two parvalbumin (Pvalb) genes: one, annotated as being related to zebrafish 'pvalb8', is enriched 22.8-fold; the other, annotated as being related to zebrafish 'pvalb3', is enriched 2.1-fold (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: Parvalbumins are cytosolic EF-hand Ca2+-buffering proteins.
source: Parvalbumins are cytosolic EF-hand Ca2+-buffering proteins (Schwaller, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Ca2+ is essential for multiple aspects of hair cell function.
source: Ca2+ is essential for multiple aspects of hair cell function (Lenzi and Roberts, 1994; Mammano et al., 2007; Ceriani and Mammano, 2012) and different hair cell subtypes are distinguished by different complements of EF-hand Ca2+ buffers, including different parvalbumin family members.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different hair cell subtypes are distinguished by different complements of EF-hand Ca2+ buffers, including different parvalbumin family members.
source: Ca2+ is essential for multiple aspects of hair cell function (Lenzi and Roberts, 1994; Mammano et al., 2007; Ceriani and Mammano, 2012) and different hair cell subtypes are distinguished by different complements of EF-hand Ca2+ buffers, including different parvalbumin family members.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mammals have a single alpha-parvalbumin, encoded by Pvalb, and a single beta-parvalbumin, oncomodulin, encoded by Ocm.
source: Mammals have a single alpha-parvalbumin, encoded by Pvalb, and a single beta-parvalbumin, oncomodulin, encoded by Ocm (Schwaller, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Alpha-parvalbumin is restricted to cochlear inner hair cells in mammals.
source: Alpha-parvalbumin is restricted to cochlear inner hair cells, while oncomodulin is restricted to cochlear outer hair cells, and is also expressed in vestibular hair cells (Sakaguchi et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2004; Simmons et al., 2010; Pangršič et al., 2015; Tong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Oncomodulin is restricted to cochlear outer hair cells in mammals, and is also expressed in vestibular hair cells.
source: Alpha-parvalbumin is restricted to cochlear inner hair cells, while oncomodulin is restricted to cochlear outer hair cells, and is also expressed in vestibular hair cells (Sakaguchi et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2004; Simmons et al., 2010; Pangršič et al., 2015; Tong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Non-mammalian species have variable numbers of parvalbumin genes (nine in zebrafish).
source: Non-mammalian species have variable numbers of parvalbumin genes (nine in zebrafish; Friedberg, 2005), and the nomenclature for both genes and proteins is inconsistent and confusing.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of selected vertebrate parvalbumin proteins revealed three distinct clades: one comprising the alpha-parvalbumins, and two containing beta-parvalbumins.
source: This revealed three distinct clades: one comprising the alpha-parvalbumins (including zebrafish 'Pvalb6' and 'Pvalb7'; Friedberg, 2005), and two containing beta-parvalbumins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: One of the beta-parvalbumin clades includes the oncomodulins, chicken Pvalb3/thymic CPV3, bullfrog Pvalb3 and zebrafish 'Pvalb8' and 'Pvalb9'.
source: One of the beta-parvalbumin clades includes the oncomodulins (i.e., mammalian beta-parvalbumins), chicken Pvalb3/thymic CPV3 (encoded by Ocm) (Hapak et al., 1994), bullfrog Pvalb3 (Heller et al., 2002) and zebrafish 'Pvalb8' and 'Pvalb9', which were originally named Pvalb3a and Pvalb3b owing to their similarity to chicken Pvalb3/CPV3 and oncomodulin (Hsiao et al., 2002; Friedberg, 2005) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous research.

claim: The second beta-parvalbumin clade includes chicken thymic Pvalb, zebrafish 'Pvalb1-5' and various other beta-parvalbumins.
source: The second beta-parvalbumin clade includes chicken thymic Pvalb (avian thymic hormone, encoded by Ocm2) (Brewer et al., 1989), zebrafish 'Pvalb1-5' (Friedberg, 2005) and various other beta-parvalbumins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous research.

claim: Both lateral line-enriched Pvalb genes in paddlefish encode beta-parvalbumins.
source: Following our phylogenetic analysis, it was clear that both lateral line-enriched Pvalb genes encode beta-parvalbumins.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis performed.

claim: The most highly lateral line-enriched parvalbumin gene in paddlefish was named Pvalbβ1/Ocm because the predicted protein groups in the beta-parvalbumin clade containing mammalian oncomodulins.
source: We named the most highly lateral line-enriched gene Pvalbβ1/Ocm (22.8-fold enriched; 'pvalb8' in Supplementary file 1), because the predicted protein groups in the beta-parvalbumin clade containing mammalian oncomodulins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Paddlefish Pvalbβ1/Ocm is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Pvalbβ1/Ocm is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 'Pvalb8' was reported to be the most highly expressed transcript in skate ampullary organs.
source: Interestingly, 'Pvalb8' was reported to be the most highly expressed transcript in skate ampullary organs: the authors suggest that, following the voltage-dependent Ca2+ influx via Cav1.3 that depolarizes the electroreceptor and activates BK, this parvalbumin could bind Ca2+, thus blocking BK-mediated hyperpolarization and enabling further oscillations (Bellono et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The less highly lateral line-enriched parvalbumin gene in paddlefish was named Pvalbβ2 as it falls into the second beta-parvalbumin clade.
source: We named the less highly lateral line-enriched gene Pvalbβ2 (2.1-fold enriched; 'pvalb3' in Supplementary file 1), as it falls into the second beta-parvalbumin clade (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At all stages examined, paddlefish Pvalbβ2 is expressed in ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
source: At all stages examined, Pvalbβ2 proved to be expressed in ampullary organs but not neuromasts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In addition to Neurod4, Pvalbβ2 is another transcript expressed by ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
source: Therefore, in addition to Neurod4, we have identified another transcript expressed by ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
evidence: This is based on the in situ hybridization data presented.

claim: Pvalbβ2 is likely to be involved in ampullary organ-specific aspects of Ca2+ regulation.
source: We suggest that this beta-parvalbumin is likely to be involved in ampullary organ-specific aspects of Ca2+ regulation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential expression pattern and known function of parvalbumins.

claim: Two highly lateral line-enriched shaker-related voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes were found in the paddlefish dataset: Kcna5, encoding the pore-forming alpha subunit of Kv1.5 (12.4-fold enriched) and Kcnab3, encoding the beta subunit Kvβ3 (21.4-fold enriched).
source: Hence, we were very interested to find two highly lateral line-enriched shaker-related voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes in our paddlefish dataset: Kcna5, encoding the pore-forming alpha subunit of Kv1.5 (12.4-fold enriched) and Kcnab3, encoding the beta subunit Kvβ3 (21.4-fold enriched).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis data.

claim: In contrast to Cacna1d and Cacnb2, which are expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, Kcna5 and Kcnab3 are only expressed in ampullary organs.
source: In contrast to the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel subunit genes Cacna1d and Cacnb2, which are expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 4C,D), Kcna5 (Figure 6A–D) and Kcnab3 (Figure 6E–H) are only expressed in ampullary organs.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Expression of both Kcna5 and Kcnab3 is first seen around stages 38-39, slightly after the eruption of the first ampullary organs at the surface at stage 37.
source: Expression of both genes is first seen around stages 38–39, slightly after the eruption of the first ampullary organs at the surface at stage 37 (Modrell et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data and a citation to previous research.

claim: In the cardiac atrium, Kv1.5 channels are thought to conduct the 'ultra-rapid delayed rectifier' current (IKur), with relatively slow inactivation properties, which contributes to repolarization.
source: In the cardiac atrium, Kv1.5 channels are thought to conduct the 'ultra-rapid delayed rectifier' current (IKur), with relatively slow inactivation properties, which contributes to repolarization (Schmitt et al., 2014; Wettwer and Terlau, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When human KCNA5 and KCNAB3 are heterologously co-expressed in cell culture, they form a novel Kv channel that mediates very fast-inactivating (A-type) outward currents upon depolarization.
source: Furthermore, when human KCNA5 and KCNAB3 are heterologously co-expressed in cell culture, they form a novel Kv channel that, upon depolarization, mediates very fast-inactivating (A-type) outward currents (Leicher et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It is possible that Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 in paddlefish ampullary organs together constitute a rapidly-inactivating voltage-gated potassium channel that conducts an ultra-rapid delayed rectifier current.
source: Hence, it is possible that Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 in paddlefish ampullary organs together constitute a rapidly-inactivating voltage-gated potassium channel that conducts an ultra-rapid delayed rectifier current.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the expression pattern and known properties of these channel subunits.

claim: The properties of Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 would plausibly be optimal for rapid oscillation of the basal electroreceptor membrane.
source: These properties would plausibly be optimal for rapid oscillation of the basal electroreceptor membrane.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known properties of these channels.

claim: Noisy voltage oscillations have been recorded from ampullary organ canals in adult paddlefish in vivo.
source: Noisy voltage oscillations have been recorded from ampullary organ canals in adult paddlefish in vivo (Neiman and Russell, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Until now, the only evidence for the existence of a rectifying Kv channel in non-teleost ampullary organs has been from current- and voltage-clamp approaches in dissected skate ampullary organs.
source: Importantly, the only evidence until now for the existence of a rectifying Kv channel in non-teleost ampullary organs has been from current- and voltage-clamp approaches in dissected skate (cartilaginous fish) ampullary organs (Bennett and Obara, 1986; Lu and Fishman, 1995; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology research.

claim: The gene expression data suggest that the rectifying Kv channel also exists in a chondrostean fish, supporting the hypothesis that non-teleost electroreceptor physiology is conserved.
source: Our gene expression data suggest that this channel also exists in a chondrostean fish, supporting the hypothesis that non-teleost electroreceptor physiology is conserved (at least across jawed vertebrates), and identify Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 as the candidate channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data and previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 are identified as the candidate rectifying Kv channel in non-teleost ampullary organs.
source: Our gene expression data suggest that this channel also exists in a chondrostean fish, supporting the hypothesis that non-teleost electroreceptor physiology is conserved (at least across jawed vertebrates), and identify Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 as the candidate channel.
evidence: This is based on the gene expression data showing ampullary organ-specific expression.

claim: The sequence of paddlefish Kcna5 predicts several amino acid substitutions in highly conserved regions of Kv1.5 that could affect its properties.
source: The sequence of paddlefish Kcna5 predicts several amino acid substitutions in highly conserved regions of Kv1.5 that could affect its properties.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the cloned gene.

claim: The S4 segment of voltage-gated ion channels is the voltage sensor and is highly conserved.
source: The S4 segment of voltage-gated ion channels is the voltage sensor, and is highly conserved (Barros et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In paddlefish Kv1.5, the first positively-charged amino acid in the voltage sensor (R1 position) has been replaced by a threonine (T357).
source: The first positively-charged amino acid in the voltage sensor is normally arginine: since it is the first arginine in S4, it is referred to as the R1 position. In paddlefish Kv1.5, this has been replaced by a threonine (T357).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Experimental substitution of methionine at the R1 site in Drosophila Shaker decreases the gating charge on the channel and the slope of the conductance voltage curve.
source: Experimental substitution of methionine at this site in Drosophila Shaker (R362M; Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996) decreases the gating charge on the channel and the slope of the conductance voltage curve (Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996; Elliott et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: R1 forms a seal with hydrophobic residues in S2 that keeps ions from flowing around the S4 segment.
source: Aside from its role as part of the voltage sensor, R1 forms a seal with hydrophobic residues in S2 that keeps ions from flowing around the S4 segment: substitution of R1 in Drosophila Shaker with histidine (R362H) allows protons to leak past S4 (Starace and Bezanilla, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Substitution of R1 in Drosophila Shaker with some amino acids allows monovalent cations to leak past S4 when the cell is hyperpolarized (omega current).
source: Substitution with some other amino acids (alanine, cysteine, serine, valine) allows monovalent cations to leak past S4 when the cell is hyperpolarized (omega current) (Tombola et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It is not known if a threonine at the R1 position would encourage an omega current, but an omega current could act like a slow depolarizing leak current, possibly contributing to the spontaneous activity of ampullary electroreceptors.
source: It is not known if a threonine at this position would encourage an omega current, but an omega current could act like a slow depolarizing leak current, possibly contributing to the spontaneous activity of ampullary electroreceptors.
evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of omega currents.

claim: A variety of studies indicate that the end of the S3/S4 linker and the top of S4 contact the top of S2, S3 and S5/pore in the closed or open state.
source: A variety of studies indicate that the end of the S3/S4 linker and the top of S4 contact the top of S2, S3 and S5/pore in the closed or open state (Kanevsky and Aldrich, 1999; Elliott et al., 2004; Soler-Llavina et al., 2006; Henrion et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2011; Elliott et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Generally speaking, amino acid substitutions at some of these positions cause a rightward shift in the conductance-voltage curve, meaning that the channel would open at more depolarized voltages.
source: Generally speaking, amino acid substitutions at some of these amino acid positions cause a rightward shift in the conductance-voltage curve, meaning that the channel would open at more depolarized voltages.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Characterization of the effects on Kv1.5 of the various amino acid substitutions in paddlefish will require future channel expression in a heterologous system and mutagenesis studies.
source: Characterization of the effects on Kv1.5 of these various amino acid substitutions will require future paddlefish channel expression in a heterologous system and mutagenesis studies: for example, characterizing the properties of paddlefish Kv1.5, as compared with paddlefish Kv1.5 in which these amino acids (in different combinations) have been substituted with conserved residues, and/or substituting the paddlefish-specific amino acids into, for example, human Kv1.5.
evidence: This is a statement about future experimental approaches needed.

claim: Genes that are required for synaptic transmission at the hair cell (but not photoreceptor) ribbon synapse are also expressed in larval paddlefish ampullary organs.
source: Furthermore, genes that are required for synaptic transmission at the hair cell (but not photoreceptor) ribbon synapse are also expressed in larval paddlefish ampullary organs.
evidence: This is based on the gene expression data presented in the study.

claim: The data suggest very close developmental and, most likely, evolutionary links between hair cells and electroreceptors.
source: This suggests very close developmental and, most likely, evolutionary links between hair cells and electroreceptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the shared gene expression patterns.

claim: The selective pressure for the evolution of electroreceptors is likely related to the transition from filter-feeding to predation in the lineage leading to vertebrates.
source: The selective pressure for the evolution of electroreceptors, which enable the detection of living animals in water, is likely related to the transition from filter-feeding to predation in the lineage leading to vertebrates (Gans and Northcutt, 1983; Northcutt and Gans, 1983; Northcutt, 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Various lines of evidence support the homology of all non-teleost electroreceptors, including those of lampreys.
source: Various lines of evidence support the homology of all non-teleost electroreceptors, including those of lampreys: their stimulation by weak, low-frequency cathodal fields (and inhibition by strong cathodal fields); their innervation by pre-otic anterior lateral afferents projecting to the dorsal octavolateral nucleus in the hindbrain; and, in jawed vertebrates, their demonstrated embryonic origin, together with neuromasts, from lateral line placodes (Bullock et al., 1983; Northcutt, 1992; Braun, 1996; New, 1997; Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The striking similarities in both development and physiology identified in paddlefish ampullary organs are consistent with electroreceptor evolution in the vertebrate ancestor either via the diversification of hair cells that had already evolved from ancestral mechanoreceptor cells, or via the diversification of an ancestral mechanoreceptor cell into both hair cells and electroreceptors.
source: Given this, the striking similarities in both development and physiology that we have identified in paddlefish ampullary organs are consistent with electroreceptor evolution in the vertebrate ancestor either via the diversification of hair cells that had already evolved from ancestral mechanoreceptor cells (Duncan and Fritzsch, 2012; Fritzsch and Straka, 2014), or via the diversification of an ancestral mechanoreceptor cell - with an apical primary cilium (lost in lamprey electroreceptors), microvilli, and synaptic ribbons (Northcutt, 1986; Bodznick, 1989; New, 1997), and using otoferlin, Vglut3 and Cav1.3 channels for synaptic transmission - into both hair cells and electroreceptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The unbiased RNA-seq approach has shed new light on molecular mechanisms underlying ampullary organ development and physiology in a non-teleost chondrostean fish.
source: Our unbiased RNA-seq approach has shed new light on molecular mechanisms underlying ampullary organ development and physiology in a non-teleost chondrostean fish.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the overall contribution of the study.

claim: The expression in ampullary organs of key hair cell transcription factor genes and genes encoding proteins specifically required for glutamate release at the hair cell ribbon synapse supports close developmental and physiological, hence evolutionary, relationships between electroreceptors and hair cells.
source: The expression in ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, of key hair cell transcription factor genes, such as Atoh1, Sox2 and Pou4f3, and genes encoding proteins specifically required for glutamate release at the hair cell ribbon synapse, such as otoferlin, Vglut3 and Cav1.3 channels, supports close developmental and physiological, hence evolutionary, relationships between electroreceptors and hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data.

claim: The identification of the first-reported ampullary organ-specific genes provides novel insight into the potential molecular basis of ampullary organ-specific development and physiology.
source: Our identification of the first-reported ampullary organ-specific genes, including the proneural transcription factor gene Neurod4, a beta-parvalbumin gene, and voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes, provides novel insight into the potential molecular basis of ampullary organ-specific development and physiology.
evidence: This is based on the identification of differentially expressed genes in the study.

claim: Cav1.3 (with Cavβ2) is identified as a candidate for the apical voltage-sensing channel in paddlefish ampullary organs.
source: We identify Cav1.3 (with Cavβ2) as a candidate for the apical voltage-sensing channel (indeed, Cav1.3 was recently shown to be the voltage-sensing channel in skate electroreceptors; Bellono et al., 2017), and Kv1.5 (with unusual amino acid substitutions that may affect its properties), together with Kvβ3, as a candidate for the basal membrane rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology.
evidence: This is based on the gene expression data and supported by a recent study in skate.

claim: Kv1.5 (with unusual amino acid substitutions that may affect its properties), together with Kvβ3, is identified as a candidate for the basal membrane rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology.
source: We identify Cav1.3 (with Cavβ2) as a candidate for the apical voltage-sensing channel (indeed, Cav1.3 was recently shown to be the voltage-sensing channel in skate electroreceptors; Bellono et al., 2017), and Kv1.5 (with unusual amino acid substitutions that may affect its properties), together with Kvβ3, as a candidate for the basal membrane rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology.
evidence: This is based on the gene expression data and previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: The analysis has provided wide-ranging insights into molecular aspects of ampullary organ development and physiology, and an essential framework for future comparative work.
source: Overall, our analysis has provided wide-ranging insights into molecular aspects of ampullary organ development and physiology, and an essential framework for future comparative work to determine both the function of these genes, and the extent to which they are conserved across other non-teleost electroreceptive vertebrate groups.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the overall contribution of the study.
